milestones.title: Imperial Contradictions: Sykes-Picot Agreement & The Balfour Declaration
milestones.imageCaption: Original 2 November 1917 Balfour Declaration letter promising British support for a "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine.
milestones.mapCaption: League of Nations Mandate for Palestine (1922), showing British Mandate borders west of the River Jordan.
milestones.catalyst: During the First World War Britain sought allies against the Ottoman Empire, promising Arab independence (McMahon-Hussein) while planning Anglo-French spheres (Sykes-Picot).
milestones.turningPoint: In November 1917 Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour pledged British support for a "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine alongside existing non-Jewish civil and religious rights.
milestones.impact: Locked Britain into contradictory obligations to Arab nationalists and Zionists under the 1922 Mandate, culminating in the 1936–39 Arab Revolt and the 1939 White Paper immigration cap.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Britain’s 1939 White Paper cap on Jewish immigration collided after 1945 with desperate Holocaust survivors, driving armed Zionist groups to attack British Mandate rule at the King David Hotel.

keyTerms.definition: Core specification concept anchored to Imperial Contradictions: Sykes-Picot Agreement & The Balfour Declaration.
A secret 1916 pact between Britain and France dividing Ottoman Arab lands into European spheres of influence.
A 1917 letter from British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour declaring support for a Jewish national home in Palestine.
An authorization granted by the League of Nations to a European power to govern a former Ottoman territory until independence.

milestones.title: The Bombing of the King David Hotel, Jerusalem
milestones.imageCaption: The collapsed south-west wing of the King David Hotel housing British Mandate headquarters after the July 1946 Irgun bombing.
milestones.mapCaption: British Mandate Palestine (1945–1947), where 100,000 British troops faced an escalating post-war insurgency.
milestones.catalyst: Post-war Britain kept strict immigration limits despite US President Truman’s appeal to admit 100,000 Holocaust survivors, and raided Jewish Agency offices in Operation Agatha.
milestones.turningPoint: Irgun fighters led by Menachem Begin detonated milk churns packed with explosives beneath the King David Hotel’s south wing, killing 91 British, Arab, and Jewish people.
milestones.impact: Ended Haganah–Irgun cooperation, forced British officials into fortified "Bevingrad" security zones, and deepened pressure in London to hand Palestine to the United Nations.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Mounting casualties and war debt pushed Britain to refer Palestine to the UN in February 1947, before the summer crises of the SS Exodus and the Sergeants Affair destroyed remaining British support for the Mandate.

keyTerms.definition: British policy capping Jewish immigration into Palestine at 1,500 per month, enforced by Ernest Bevin after 1945 despite 250,000 Holocaust survivors in DP camps.
Core specification concept anchored to The Bombing of the King David Hotel, Jerusalem.
British military and administrative headquarters in Jerusalem bombed by the Irgun in July 1946 with 91 killed, shattering British public support for the Mandate.
Underground Zionist paramilitary group led by Menachem Begin that waged armed insurgency against British rule in Palestine.

milestones.title: The SS Exodus Crisis & The Sergeants Affair
milestones.specTag: International Outrage & Collapse of the Mandate
milestones.imageCaption: The damaged immigrant ship Exodus 1947 carrying roughly 4,500 Holocaust survivors at Haifa harbour after interception by the Royal Navy, July 1947.
milestones.mapCaption: British Mandate Palestine during the UNSCOP investigation in the summer of 1947.
milestones.catalyst: The Royal Navy intercepted 4,500 Holocaust survivors aboard the SS Exodus off Palestine and eventually returned them to camps in British-occupied Germany.
milestones.turningPoint: That same month Irgun militants kidnapped and hanged two British Army sergeants near Netanya in retaliation for British executions of three Irgun prisoners.
milestones.impact: Global sympathy surged for Jewish statehood after the Exodus while British press outrage over the hanged sergeants convinced Parliament to announce full withdrawal by May 1948.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Witnessing both the Exodus crisis and Britain’s refusal to stay, the UN committee (UNSCOP) recommended partitioning Palestine, leading to the historic General Assembly vote of 29 November 1947.
keyAgents: The United Nations (UNGA, UNSC, UNEF & UNRWA)

milestones.title: UN Resolution 181: The Partition Plan
milestones.specTag: The Diplomatic Catalyst for Civil War
milestones.imageCaption: UN Resolution 181 Partition Plan (29 November 1947), proposing independent Jewish and Arab states with Jerusalem under international UN trusteeship.
milestones.mapCaption: UN Resolution 181 (29 Nov 1947): proposed Jewish state (~55–56%, including the Negev), Arab state, and internationalised Jerusalem.
milestones.catalyst: UNSCOP concluded that Jewish and Palestinian Arab national claims could not be reconciled inside one state after Britain handed the Mandate problem to the UN.
milestones.turningPoint: The UN General Assembly passed Resolution 181 (33 votes to 13), allocating ~55–56% of Mandate Palestine to a Jewish state, the remainder to an Arab state, and Jerusalem to UN control.
milestones.impact: Jewish Agency leaders accepted reluctantly to gain sovereign statehood for survivors, whereas the Arab Higher Committee rejected giving over half the land to one-third of the population; civil war erupted within days.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Months of escalating civil war — including Haganah offensives under Plan Dalet, Deir Yassin, and mass Palestinian flight — meant that Britain’s exit on 14 May 1948 immediately turned civil conflict into a regional war.
keyAgents: The United Nations (UNGA, UNSC, UNEF & UNRWA)

keyTerms.definition: The November 1947 UN General Assembly vote to partition Palestine into separate Jewish (56%) and Arab (43%) states with an internationalised Jerusalem.
Core specification concept anchored to UN Resolution 181: The Partition Plan.
The official governing leadership of the Yishuv in Palestine, led by David Ben-Gurion, which campaigned for statehood and accepted the 1947 UN Partition Plan.
Core specification concept anchored to UN Resolution 181: The Partition Plan.

milestones.title: Declaration of the State of Israel & Outbreak of the 1948–49 War
milestones.imageCaption: David Ben-Gurion proclaiming the establishment of the State of Israel in Tel Aviv beneath Theodor Herzl’s portrait, 14 May 1948.
milestones.mapCaption: The 1948–49 Arab-Israeli War and resulting 1949 Green Line armistice borders.
milestones.catalyst: The last British High Commissioner sailed from Haifa on 14 May 1948, ending the British Mandate amid fierce Jewish–Arab civil fighting.
milestones.turningPoint: David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel on 14 May; at dawn on 15 May armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon entered Palestine.
milestones.impact: Israel fought for survival at birth while Arab states aimed to prevent partition; unified IDF command, June UN truce rearmament via Czechoslovakia, and Arab disunity gave Israel victory.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Israeli counter-offensives expanded Israel’s control well beyond the UN partition boundaries, reshaping the map in the 1949 Armistice Agreements and leaving over 700,000 Palestinians displaced.

milestones.title: 1949 Armistice Agreements, Territorial Changes & The Refugee Crisis
milestones.imageCaption: Palestinian Arab refugees displaced during the 1948–49 war; over 700,000 fled or were expelled into neighbouring territories.
milestones.mapCaption: The 1949 Green Line Armistice Borders: Israel held 78% of former Mandate Palestine, Jordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt administered Gaza.
milestones.catalyst: Decisive IDF counter-offensives in late 1948 brought Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan, and Syria into UN-mediated armistice talks on Rhodes in 1949.
milestones.turningPoint: The 1949 Armistice Agreements drew the "Green Line": Israel held 78% of Mandate Palestine, Jordan annexed the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt administered Gaza.
milestones.impact: Over 700,000 Palestinian refugees remained barred from returning while Israel absorbed waves of European and Mizrahi Jewish immigrants under the 1950 Law of Return.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Unresolved armistice borders, fedayeen raids from Gaza, and Israel’s heavy February 1955 Gaza Raid pushed Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser to seek Soviet-bloc weapons and confront Britain, France, and Israel over Suez.
keyAgents: The United Nations (UNGA, UNSC, UNEF & UNRWA)

keyTerms.definition: Core specification concept anchored to 1949 Armistice Agreements, Territorial Changes & The Refugee Crisis.
Arabic for "The Catastrophe", referring to the mass displacement of over 700,000 Palestinian Arabs during the 1948–49 War.
United Nations Relief and Works Agency, founded in December 1949 to provide emergency food, relief, and shelter to Palestinian refugees.
1950 Israeli Knesset legislation granting every Jewish person worldwide the inherent legal right to settle in Israel and receive citizenship.

milestones.title: The Suez Crisis & The Rise of Gamal Abdel Nasser
milestones.imageCaption: Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser greeted by crowds in 1956 as the champion of Pan-Arab nationalism.
milestones.mapCaption: The 1956 Suez Crisis: Israeli advance across Sinai and Anglo-French landings at Port Said before US-enforced withdrawal.
milestones.catalyst: After Israel’s 1955 Gaza Raid and Nasser’s Czechoslovak arms deal, the USA and Britain cancelled loans for Egypt’s Aswan High Dam.
milestones.turningPoint: Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company in July 1956; Britain, France, and Israel secretly colluded to invade Sinai and the Canal Zone in October–November.
milestones.impact: US financial pressure forced Anglo-French and Israeli withdrawal; UNEF troops entered Sinai, Israel gained shipping via Tiran, and Nasser became the hero of Pan-Arabism.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Nasser’s Pan-Arab leadership after Suez created intense pressure on Egypt to confront Israel’s Jordan water project in 1964, leading to the Cairo Summit and the founding of the PLO.

keyTerms.definition: A 1955 agreement where the Soviet bloc supplied Egypt with massive amounts of advanced weaponry, shocking the West.
The transfer of a major branch of industry or commerce from private to state ownership or control (e.g., the Suez Canal).
Core specification concept anchored to The Suez Crisis & The Rise of Gamal Abdel Nasser.
Core specification concept anchored to The Suez Crisis & The Rise of Gamal Abdel Nasser.

milestones.title: The Cairo Summit, Jordan Water Dispute & Creation of the PLO
milestones.specTag: Water Rivalry, Border Raids & Rising Tension
milestones.imageCaption: Arab heads of state meeting at the January 1964 Cairo Summit to coordinate water diversion plans and establish the PLO.
milestones.mapCaption: Pre-June 1967 borders where Jordan River headwater clashes, Fatah raids, and the 1966 Samu reprisal unfolded.
milestones.catalyst: Israel opened its National Water Carrier from the Sea of Galilee in 1964, prompting Arab states to convene in Cairo to plan headwater diversions.
milestones.turningPoint: The Arab League backed the founding of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) in May 1964, while Yasser Arafat’s Fatah launched Syrian-backed raids into Israel from 1965.
milestones.impact: Cross-border guerrilla attacks, Israel’s November 1966 reprisal at Samu in Jordan, and the April 1967 Syrian-Israeli air battle pushed the region to the brink of war.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Escalating Syrian border clashes and a false May 1967 Soviet warning of an Israeli invasion plan led Nasser to expel UNEF and close the Straits of Tiran, triggering the Six-Day War.

keyTerms.definition: Core specification concept anchored to The Cairo Summit, Jordan Water Dispute & Creation of the PLO.
A major Israeli infrastructure network completed in 1964 to pump water from the Sea of Galilee across the country.
A Palestinian nationalist guerrilla organisation founded by Yasser Arafat that launched armed cross-border raids into Israel.
A large-scale Israeli military reprisal raid into the West Bank village of Samu in November 1966 following a landmine attack.

milestones.title: The Six-Day War: Pre-Emptive Strike & Conquered Territories
milestones.imageCaption: David Rubinger’s photograph of Israeli paratroopers at the Western Wall in Jerusalem’s Old City, 7 June 1967.
milestones.mapCaption: Territories captured by Israel in June 1967: Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights.
milestones.catalyst: In May 1967 Nasser expelled UNEF peacekeepers from Sinai, closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, and signed a defence pact with Jordan.
milestones.turningPoint: On 5 June Israel launched a pre-emptive air strike that destroyed Arab air forces on the ground in hours, before defeating Egyptian, Jordanian, and Syrian armies.
milestones.impact: Israel captured Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights in six days, placing around one million Palestinians under military occupation.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Israel’s sweeping territorial conquests forced the Arab League at Khartoum and the UN Security Council in New York to clash over the terms of any future peace.

keyTerms.definition: A narrow maritime passage into the Gulf of Aqaba blockaded by Egypt, threatening Israel's southern port of Eilat.
Core specification concept anchored to The Six-Day War: Pre-Emptive Strike & Conquered Territories.
Core specification concept anchored to The Six-Day War: Pre-Emptive Strike & Conquered Territories.
The territory west of the River Jordan, administered by Jordan from 1948 until captured by Israel in June 1967.

milestones.title: The Khartoum "Three Noes" & UN Security Council Resolution 242
milestones.imageCaption: Official United Nations Security Council text of Resolution 242, adopted unanimously on 22 November 1967.
milestones.mapCaption: Post-1967 Occupied Territories at the centre of UN Resolution 242’s "Land for Peace" principle.
milestones.catalyst: Arab states at the September 1967 Khartoum Summit declared "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations" with Israel while Israel began strategic settlements.
milestones.turningPoint: On 22 November 1967 the UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 242, trading Israeli withdrawal from occupied territories for secure, recognised borders.
milestones.impact: Created the "Land for Peace" diplomatic benchmark, yet disputed wording ("from territories") and the referral to Palestinians only as "refugees" hardened the deadlock.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Because Arab states had lost in 1967 and Resolution 242 omitted Palestinian statehood, Arafat’s Fatah took over the PLO to wage independent guerrilla struggle from Jordan.
keyAgents: The United Nations (UNGA, UNSC, UNEF & UNRWA)

keyTerms.definition: Core specification concept anchored to The Khartoum "Three Noes" & UN Security Council Resolution 242.
A United Nations Security Council resolution passed on 22 November 1967 establishing the principle of "Land for Peace".
The diplomatic formula requiring Israel to return occupied land in exchange for Arab recognition and permanent peace.
Core specification concept anchored to The Khartoum "Three Noes" & UN Security Council Resolution 242.

milestones.title: Dawson’s Field, Black September in Jordan & The Munich Olympics
milestones.specTag: Palestinian Militancy, Jordanian Civil War & International Terrorism
milestones.imageCaption: Hijacked Western airliners blown up by the PFLP at Dawson’s Field in Jordan on 12 September 1970, triggering Black September.
milestones.mapCaption: Jordan and Israel’s post-1967 borders before the PLO’s 1970–71 expulsion from Jordan to Lebanon.
milestones.catalyst: After Karameh (1968), armed fedayeen checkpoints formed a "state within a state" in Jordan and the PFLP blew up hijacked airliners at Dawson’s Field.
milestones.turningPoint: King Hussein’s army crushed fedayeen strongholds in September 1970, repulsed Syrian tanks, and expelled the PLO to Lebanon; in 1972 Black September killed 11 Israelis at Munich.
milestones.impact: Shifted the PLO’s military base into southern Lebanon and Beirut, while Munich brought fierce Western condemnation alongside global focus on Palestinian statelessness.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Meanwhile on the Egyptian front, after the 1969–70 War of Attrition and Israel’s rejection of Anwar Sadat’s 1971 peace offer, Egypt and Syria launched a surprise war in October 1973.

keyTerms.definition: A battle in Jordan in March 1968 where Palestinian fighters resisted an Israeli armored raid, boosting Palestinian national pride.
Core specification concept anchored to Dawson’s Field, Black September in Jordan & The Munich Olympics.
A civil conflict in Jordan in September 1970 in which King Hussein's army defeated Palestinian militias and expelled the PLO.
Core specification concept anchored to Dawson’s Field, Black September in Jordan & The Munich Olympics.

milestones.title: The Yom Kippur / October War & The Arab Oil Weapon
milestones.imageCaption: Egyptian military vehicles crossing a pontoon bridge through the breached Bar-Lev sand rampart across the Suez Canal, October 1973.
milestones.mapCaption: The October 1973 Yom Kippur War: Egyptian Suez crossing, Syrian Golan assault, and US-resupplied Israeli counter-offensives.
milestones.catalyst: Determined to overturn the 1967 status quo after his 1971 peace initiative failed, Egypt’s Anwar Sadat forged a secret war plan with Syria.
milestones.turningPoint: On 6 October 1973 Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal and breached the Bar-Lev Line under SAM missile cover while Syria attacked Golan, before US-airlifted IDF counter-attacks.
milestones.impact: Shattered beliefs in Israeli invulnerability, triggered OAPEC’s oil embargo quadrupling oil prices, and sparked a brief US–Soviet nuclear alert ending in UN Resolution 338.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Shocked by quadrupled oil prices and October’s superpower nuclear alert, US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger immediately launched Shuttle Diplomacy to separate the rival armies.

keyTerms.definition: A static border conflict along the Suez Canal from 1969 to 1970 involving heavy artillery duels, commando raids, and air dogfights.
A fortified chain of Israeli concrete bunkers and massive sixty-foot sand ramparts built along the eastern bank of the Suez Canal.
Core specification concept anchored to The Yom Kippur / October War & The Arab Oil Weapon.
Core specification concept anchored to The Yom Kippur / October War & The Arab Oil Weapon.

milestones.title: Kissinger’s "Shuttle Diplomacy" & Reopening of the Suez Canal
milestones.specTag: Step-by-Step Disengagement & Ending the Oil Embargo
milestones.imageCaption: Egyptian and Israeli military negotiators meeting under UN auspices at Kilometre 101 on the Cairo–Suez road.
milestones.mapCaption: Sinai and Golan disengagement buffer zones negotiated during Henry Kissinger’s 1974–75 Shuttle Diplomacy.
milestones.catalyst: The OAPEC oil embargo and October 1973 superpower nuclear alert convinced Washington to lead direct step-by-step mediation.
milestones.turningPoint: US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger shuttled between Cairo, Jerusalem, and Damascus to broker Sinai I, Golan, and Sinai II pullbacks; Egypt reopened the Suez Canal in June 1975.
milestones.impact: Ended the Arab oil embargo in March 1974, stabilised the Sinai and Golan fronts, and drew Sadat’s Egypt away from Moscow toward US partnership.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Because Kissinger’s step-by-step diplomacy bypassed the Palestinians, Arab states at Rabat backed the PLO, setting up Yasser Arafat’s landmark UN address in November 1974.
keyAgents: The United Nations (UNGA, UNSC, UNEF & UNRWA)

keyTerms.definition: The diplomatic method pioneered by US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger in 1973–74, flying between capitals to broker peace.

milestones.title: Yasser Arafat Addresses the UN General Assembly
milestones.imageCaption: PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat addressing the UN General Assembly on 13 November 1974 ("an olive branch and a freedom fighter’s gun").
milestones.mapCaption: Post-1973 Middle East as the Arab League and UN General Assembly recognised the PLO’s claim to represent Palestinians.
milestones.catalyst: In October 1974 the Arab League’s Rabat Summit recognised the PLO — rather than Jordan — as the "sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people".
milestones.turningPoint: Arafat addressed the UN General Assembly urging the world not to let "the olive branch fall from my hand", and the UN granted the PLO observer status.
milestones.impact: Transformed the Palestinian cause at the UN from a refugee question into a recognised political claim to self-determination, though Israel and the USA still barred PLO talks.
milestones.bridgeToNext: With comprehensive multi-party talks blocked over PLO representation and Egypt hit by 1977 bread riots, Sadat shocked the world by flying directly to Jerusalem.

milestones.title: President Anwar Sadat’s Historic Visit to Jerusalem
milestones.imageCaption: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin conversing in Jerusalem during Sadat’s November 1977 visit.
milestones.mapCaption: Egypt and Israeli-occupied Sinai on the eve of Sadat’s November 1977 peace mission to Jerusalem.
milestones.catalyst: Crippling defence spending and Egypt’s January 1977 bread riots convinced Sadat that Egypt needed peace, US aid, and the full return of Sinai’s oilfields.
milestones.turningPoint: Welcomed by Likud Prime Minister Menachem Begin, Sadat flew to Jerusalem and addressed the Knesset, offering peace and recognition alongside demands for full 1967 withdrawal.
milestones.impact: Shattered a thirty-year taboo against face-to-face Arab–Israeli diplomacy, although follow-up talks soon stalled over Sinai settlements and Palestinian self-rule.
milestones.bridgeToNext: When bilateral talks deadlocked in 1978 over Israeli settlements and the West Bank, US President Jimmy Carter invited Sadat and Begin to Camp David to save the peace initiative.

milestones.title: The Camp David Accords
milestones.imageCaption: Menachem Begin, Jimmy Carter, and Anwar Sadat at the Camp David presidential retreat in Maryland, September 1978.
milestones.mapCaption: Sinai, Gaza, and the West Bank — the territories debated across thirteen days at Camp David in September 1978.
milestones.catalyst: Egyptian–Israeli talks risked collapse over dismantling Israeli settlements in Sinai and Begin’s opposition to an independent Palestinian state.
milestones.turningPoint: President Jimmy Carter mediated thirteen days of closed talks at Camp David, agreeing full Sinai return for peace plus a vague five-year "autonomy" framework for the West Bank and Gaza.
milestones.impact: Won Sadat and Begin the Nobel Peace Prize and unlocked bilateral peace, but Arab states and the PLO rejected the autonomy language because Palestinians had no seat.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Backed by pledges of billions of dollars in annual US aid and personal shuttle visits by Carter in early 1979, the Camp David framework became the binding Treaty of Washington.

milestones.title: The Treaty of Washington: Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty Signed
milestones.imageCaption: Sadat, Carter, and Begin join hands on the White House Lawn after signing the Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty, 26 March 1979.
milestones.mapCaption: Regional map following the 1979 Egypt–Israel Treaty: phased Israeli withdrawal from Sinai completed by April 1982.
milestones.catalyst: Carter’s March 1979 mediation settled final treaty timetables and secured major long-term American economic and military aid for both countries.
milestones.turningPoint: Sadat and Begin signed the formal peace treaty in Washington: Israel withdrew all troops and settlers from Sinai in exchange for embassies, trade, and free Suez and Tiran shipping.
milestones.impact: Fulfilled "Land for Peace" between Israel and the strongest Arab military state, while leaving Palestinian self-determination in Gaza and the West Bank unresolved.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Outrage across the Arab world that Egypt had signed a separate peace without a Palestinian state triggered Egypt’s expulsion from the Arab League and fuelled the plot against Sadat’s life.

keyTerms.definition: The historic March 1979 peace treaty where Israel withdrew completely from the Sinai Peninsula in exchange for Egyptian diplomatic recognition.

milestones.title: The Arab League Boycott & Assassination of Anwar Sadat
milestones.specTag: Backlash & Survival of the Peace Treaty
milestones.imageCaption: The Unknown Soldier Memorial in Cairo opposite the parade reviewing stand where President Anwar Sadat was assassinated in October 1981.
milestones.mapCaption: Post-treaty regional alignment: peace held on Israel’s southern border with Egypt while northern clashes grew along Lebanon.
milestones.catalyst: Arab leaders at the 1979 Baghdad Summit condemned Egypt’s separate peace, imposed economic sanctions, suspended Egypt from the Arab League, and moved League HQ to Tunis.
milestones.turningPoint: On 6 October 1981 Islamist extremists inside the Egyptian army assassinated President Anwar Sadat during an October War victory parade in Cairo.
milestones.impact: Despite Sadat’s assassination and Arab isolation, Egypt upheld the 1979 treaty and Israel completed its Sinai handover in April 1982, ending the risk of a two-front conventional war.
milestones.bridgeToNext: With its southern border peaceful after April 1982, Israel’s government turned northwards two months later to launch a major invasion of Lebanon aimed at crushing the PLO.

milestones.title: The 1982 Israeli Invasion of Lebanon & Siege of Beirut
milestones.imageCaption: Israeli Defence Minister Ariel Sharon overlooking Beirut with military maps during the 1982 invasion of Lebanon.
milestones.mapCaption: The June 1982 Israeli advance to Beirut and the August 1982 sea evacuation of PLO forces to Tunis.
milestones.catalyst: Cross-border clashes along southern Lebanon (despite UNIFIL peacekeepers since 1978) peaked when splinter gunmen outside the PLO shot Israel’s ambassador in London.
milestones.turningPoint: Defence Minister Ariel Sharon drove IDF forces well beyond the 40 km border zone to surround and shell PLO headquarters in West Beirut for ten weeks.
milestones.impact: US mediation evacuated Arafat and ~14,000 PLO fighters by sea to distant Tunis, removing the PLO from Israel’s border but entangling Israel inside Lebanon.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Weeks after PLO fighters left Beirut under international pledges to protect camp civilians, the murder of Lebanon’s president led directly to the Sabra and Shatila massacre.

keyTerms.definition: Core specification concept anchored to The 1982 Israeli Invasion of Lebanon & Siege of Beirut.
The June 1982 full-scale Israeli military invasion of Lebanon commanded by Ariel Sharon to destroy the PLO's military infrastructure.

milestones.title: The Sabra and Shatila Massacre & The Kahan Commission
milestones.imageCaption: IDF Chief of Staff Rafael Eitan and Beirut commander Amos Yaron in 1982; both were censured alongside Sharon by Israel’s Kahan Commission.
milestones.mapCaption: West Beirut refugee camps and Israel’s southern Lebanon security zone following the 1982 war.
milestones.catalyst: After Lebanese Christian President-elect Bachir Gemayel was assassinated on 14 September 1982, IDF forces entered West Beirut and encircled Sabra and Shatila.
milestones.turningPoint: IDF commanders allowed allied Lebanese Phalangist militiamen into Sabra and Shatila, where Phalangists massacred hundreds to several thousand unarmed Palestinian and Lebanese civilians.
milestones.impact: Global outrage and huge Tel Aviv protests forced the Kahan Commission inquiry (1983), which found Sharon bore "indirect responsibility" and compelled his resignation as Defence Minister.
milestones.bridgeToNext: With the PLO exiled far away in Tunis and settlements expanding across the West Bank and Gaza, Palestinians living under occupation erupted in a grassroots uprising in December 1987.

keyTerms.definition: Core specification concept anchored to The Sabra and Shatila Massacre & The Kahan Commission.
Two Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut where Lebanese Christian Phalangist militias massacred hundreds of civilians in September 1982.

milestones.title: Outbreak of the First Intifada ("Shaking Off")
milestones.imageCaption: Palestinian youths confronting Israeli troops in Gaza after the First Intifada erupted in December 1987.
milestones.mapCaption: The Gaza Strip, West Bank, and East Jerusalem — occupied since 1967 — where the First Intifada spread from Jabalia camp.
milestones.catalyst: Twenty years of military rule, land seizures, and economic hardship boiled over on 8 December 1987 when an IDF lorry crash killed four Palestinian workers at Jabalia in Gaza.
milestones.turningPoint: Spontaneous protests, stone-throwing, commercial strikes, and tax boycotts spread across Gaza and the West Bank under local UNLU coordination, while Hamas formed in Gaza.
milestones.impact: Media images of Defence Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s "iron fist" crackdown damaged Israel’s image abroad and convinced leaders like Rabin that occupation required a political settlement.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Pressured by the Intifada inside the territories and Jordan’s 1988 withdrawal of its West Bank claim, Arafat moved in late 1988 to accept Resolution 242 and renounce terrorism.

keyTerms.definition: Core specification concept anchored to Outbreak of the First Intifada ("Shaking Off").
A sustained grassroots civilian uprising ("The Shaking Off") against Israeli military occupation that erupted in Gaza and the West Bank in December 1987.

milestones.title: Arafat Renounces Terrorism, Post-Cold War Shift & The Madrid Conference
milestones.specTag: US–PLO Dialogue, Gulf War Fallout & Madrid
milestones.imageCaption: US President George H. W. Bush addressing the opening of the US–Soviet co-sponsored Madrid Peace Conference, October 1991.
milestones.mapCaption: Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Golan still under post-1967 Israeli occupation during the 1988–91 diplomatic shift and Madrid Conference.
milestones.catalyst: After 1988 Soviet power collapsed, and Arafat’s backing for Iraq in the 1990–91 Gulf War cost the PLO vital Gulf Arab funding and diplomatic standing.
milestones.turningPoint: Arafat accepted Resolution 242 and renounced terrorism at Geneva (1988); in October 1991 the USA and USSR convened the Madrid Peace Conference with Israeli and Arab–Palestinian delegations.
milestones.impact: Opened historic face-to-face regional talks (with Palestinian figures like Hanan Ashrawi), though Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir still refused direct PLO negotiations.
milestones.bridgeToNext: When public post-Madrid talks stalled in Washington and Yitzhak Rabin won Israel’s 1992 election promising peace, Israeli and PLO envoys opened a secret back-channel in Oslo.

milestones.title: The Oslo I Accords (Declaration of Principles)
milestones.imageCaption: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat shake hands on the White House Lawn alongside President Bill Clinton, 13 September 1993.
milestones.mapCaption: Interim Palestinian self-rule beginning in Gaza and Jericho under Oslo I (1993–94) and expanding under Oslo II (1995).
milestones.catalyst: Norwegian mediators hosted secret direct Israel–PLO talks near Oslo while both Rabin and a financially weakened Arafat sought a deal before Hamas grew stronger.
milestones.turningPoint: Israel and the PLO exchanged Letters of Mutual Recognition and signed Oslo I in Washington, creating an interim Palestinian National Authority (PNA) starting in Gaza and Jericho.
milestones.impact: Achieved historic mutual recognition, yet postponed Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, and borders for five years while critics like Edward Said warned it left occupation intact.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Oslo I paved the way for Jordan’s 1994 peace treaty with Israel and the September 1995 Oslo II map, even as settler violence and Hamas bus bombings attacked the accords.

milestones.title: Israel–Jordan Peace Treaty, Oslo II (Areas A, B, C) & Assassination of Rabin
milestones.specTag: West Bank Zones & Crisis of the Peace Process
milestones.imageCaption: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin speaking at the Tel Aviv peace rally on 4 November 1995, minutes before his assassination.
milestones.mapCaption: Oslo II Interim Agreement (September 1995): West Bank divided into Area A (Palestinian control), Area B (joint), and Area C (~60% full Israeli control).
milestones.catalyst: Following the October 1994 Israel–Jordan Peace Treaty, negotiators worked to extend PNA self-rule into West Bank towns amid the 1994 Hebron massacre and Hamas suicide bombings.
milestones.turningPoint: Oslo II (September 1995) divided the West Bank into Areas A, B, and C; on 4 November 1995 Israeli religious-nationalist extremist Yigal Amir assassinated Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.
milestones.impact: Over 60% of the West Bank (Area C, including settlements and roads) stayed under Israeli control, and Rabin’s murder deprived Oslo of its key Israeli leader at a fragile moment.
milestones.bridgeToNext: By late 1995, unresolved final-status disputes over Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, and fragmented Area C borders — combined with Hamas bombings and Rabin’s assassination — left peace fragile and unfinished.
